fixes.explanation: A colt it is, friend. Jesus tells the two disciples they'll find one tied there, in the village ahead of them. They go and find it just as He told them (Luke 19:32).
Owners, yes! The colt's owners asked the disciples, “Why are you untying the colt?” (Luke 19:33). Somebody noticed what they were doing. Good thing the disciples already had their answer ready.
Neighbors is a fair guess, friend, but the text says owners. Luke 19:33 says, “…its owners asked…” It makes sense they'd be the ones asking. The disciples answered just the way Jesus told them.
Their cloaks, friend! Luke 19:35 says they “…threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it.” Cloaks first, then Jesus. That's the order the text gives.
Sackcloth, friend? That's a scratchy guess! It's not in this story. The disciples threw their cloaks over the colt, then put Jesus on it (Luke 19:35).
Fine linen sounds fancy, but the text doesn't mention it. What the disciples threw over the colt was their cloaks. Then they put Jesus on it (Luke 19:35). I love how plain that is.

Prophet is a good word, friend, but it's not the one that comes out of that crowd. They shout, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Luke 19:38). That's not a title you whisper. King, loud and clear.

Shepherd is a lovely title, friend, and Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd in John 10:11. But here, the crowd shouts, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Luke 19:38). King is the word they use. They said it loud, too.

Feed would've been a friendlier ask, friend. But the Pharisees say, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” That's in Luke 19:39. They weren't asking for anything on a plate, they were asking Jesus to rebuke His disciples.

The very stones! Jesus says, “I tell you, if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.” Think about that, friend. Even stones get a voice in that sentence. That's a big answer to a small request.
Trees are a good guess, friend, since they stand around all day with nothing to say. But Jesus says, “…if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.” That's Luke 19:40. Rocks, not branches.
Wept. Luke 19:41 says that as Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it. I think this one hurts a little, friend. First the crowd praises God, then the text shows Jesus weeping.
